content: The HPV vaccine is a quadrivalent recombinant vaccine designed to protect against human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is approved by the FDA for prophylactic use and is administered intramuscularly in a three-dose schedule at 0, 2, and 6 months. The vaccine must be shaken well before use to ensure proper suspension and should not be diluted or mixed with other vaccines. After agitation, the vaccine appears as a white, cloudy liquid. It is administered in the deltoid region of the upper arm or the anterolateral thigh. Common adverse reactions include injection site reactions (pain, swelling, erythema, pruritus), headache, fever, nausea, dizziness, and syncope. Syncope, sometimes associated with tonic-clonic movements or seizure-like activity, has been reported post-vaccination and may result in injury from falls. Observation for 15 minutes after administration is recommended to monitor for such events. Anaphylaxis has also been reported, necessitating the availability of appropriate medical treatment and supervision. The vaccine is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to yeast or any component of the vaccine, as well as those who experienced severe allergic reactions to a previous dose of Gardasil. It is not indicated for use in women aged 27 years or older, though safety data for women aged 16 to 45 years has been collected. Clinical trials have demonstrated the vaccine's efficacy in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grades 2/3, adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) grades 2/3, vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VaIN) grades 2/3, and external genital warts. These conditions are considered surrogate markers for the prevention of cervical, vulvar, and vaginal cancers. In men, the vaccine has shown efficacy in preventing external genital warts, penile/perineal/perianal intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) grades 1/2/3, and anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) grades 1/2/3, as well as anal cancer. The vaccine's safety profile was evaluated in clinical trials involving over 18,000 individuals. Injection site reactions were the most commonly reported adverse events, with most being mild to moderate in intensity. Serious systemic adverse reactions were rare and occurred at similar rates in the vaccine and control groups. Post-marketing surveillance has reported additional adverse events, including autoimmune hemolytic anemia, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, lymphadenopathy, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and deep vein thrombosis, though causality has not been established. The vaccine is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus or impaired fertility, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking. The vaccine should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Women who become pregnant before completing the three-dose regimen are advised to defer the remaining doses until after pregnancy. The vaccine's immunogenicity is not impaired by the use of hormonal contraceptives. However, immunosuppressive therapies, such as corticosteroids or cytotoxic drugs, may reduce the immune response to the vaccine. The vaccine has not been evaluated for use in individuals under 9 years of age, those aged 65 years and older, or those with renal or hepatic impairment. The vaccine is a non-infectious recombinant product prepared from purified virus-like particles (VLPs) of the major capsid (L1) protein of HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. These VLPs are produced in recombinant Saccharomyces cerevisiae and are adsorbed onto an aluminum-containing adjuvant (amorphous aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate). The vaccine does not contain preservatives or antibiotics. In summary, the HPV vaccine is a safe and effective prophylactic measure against HPV-related diseases, including cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers, as well as genital warts. It is well-tolerated, with most adverse reactions being mild and transient. Proper administration and post-vaccination monitoring are essential to ensure safety.
